deck: Falling task and application costs are compressing entry-level work and generic software rents while compute, energy, data, distribution and trusted workflows become scarcer and more strategic.

signal_rationale.delta: By October 2026, evidence from labour markets, software valuations, pricing models, cloud regulation and energy infrastructure can be connected into one observable shift: AI is reducing the scarcity of some cognitive tasks and application features while raising the strategic scarcity of compute, power, capital, distribution and trusted workflows.
signal_rationale.evidence: The assessment triangulates Stanford labour and investment data, ILO and OECD occupational exposure, NBER and METR productivity evidence, SEG and Stripe software-market data, Salesforce pricing, IEA physical-infrastructure data, FTC and European Commission competition work, Microsoft filings and clearly labelled investor theses.
signal_rationale.scale_path: Further diffusion depends on lower model and inference costs, reliable agentic workflows and organizational redesign; concentration depends on whether chips, electricity, grid access, cloud, proprietary data and distribution remain scale-constrained.
signal_rationale.transmission: The shift transmits through entry-level hiring, apprenticeship structures, software pricing and valuation, capital allocation, electricity systems, cloud dependence, bargaining power and international distribution of technology rents.
signal_rationale.falsifier: The thesis weakens if exposed young-worker hiring recovers while AI adoption rises, seat-based software pricing remains dominant in agentic workflows, generic application margins retain durable premiums, and cloud/compute/energy bottlenecks and concentration fall materially.

selection_rationale: The canonical Europe–Russia–Ukraine security-system report explicitly distinguishes Poland and the Baltic states because historical memory and geographic proximity make Russian military power a more immediate national-security variable. Lithuania lacks a reusable country dossier despite being a key Baltic state where defence spending, German force deployment, energy decoupling, Polish connectivity, demographics and productivity are tightly linked. Existing Russia, Poland and Germany dossiers make the Lithuanian context directly reusable.
contrary_evidence: Defence spending above 5% of GDP and proximity to Russia support a high-security-burden thesis, while euro-area membership, moderate debt, strong institutions and sustained growth argue against treating Lithuania as economically fragile.
Population decline and ageing constrain labour supply, but positive international migration and high wage growth have recently supported employment and domestic demand.

Russian electricity-system dependence has ended and LNG plus renewables have diversified supply, but imports, interconnections and storage remain necessary, so energy independence should not be described as autarky.
A small domestic market constrains scale, while lasers, fintech and higher-technology manufacturing demonstrate that deep EU integration and specialised exports can overcome some scale limits.
limitations: 2026 growth and inflation forecasts vary by source and forecast date; they are attributed rather than averaged.
The 5.38% of GDP defence figure is a budget allocation and does not directly measure military effectiveness or domestic value added.
The German brigade remains in deployment and infrastructure build-out; full operational capability is planned for 2027.
Renewable shares of domestic generation and of total electricity demand are different measures and are kept separate.
Migration and population data can be revised; positive net migration does not eliminate negative natural population change.
RRF payment requests and milestone completion do not directly measure long-run productivity outcomes.
Security framing in official Lithuanian sources reflects the state's documented policy assessment; factual capabilities and expenditures are separated from political interpretation.

selection_rationale: Portugal is an EU, euro-area and NATO member whose fiscal repair, Atlantic geography, renewable-heavy power system, tourism-dependent external balance and migration-supported labour supply create mechanisms not covered by existing France, Germany or European security dossiers. A reusable Portuguese country context is needed to analyse Iberian energy integration, Atlantic logistics and defence, southern-European productivity convergence and the post-RRF investment transition without reconstructing the same structural background.
contrary_evidence: Sharp public-debt reduction, repeated fiscal surpluses, historically low unemployment and stronger bank balance sheets support a resilience thesis, while debt remains high, ageing pressures are rising and productivity convergence remains weak.

Immigration has reversed population decline and expanded labour supply, while a very high ageing index and slower migration in 2025 show that demographic constraints have been mitigated rather than solved.

Renewables already supply most electricity consumption and can support industrial investment, while imported fuels, system-integration needs and the Iberian blackout demonstrate that electricity abundance is not equivalent to complete energy autonomy.

Housing price increases are extreme, but limited mortgage-credit expansion and stronger banks indicate that structural supply restrictions are currently a clearer mechanism than a repeat of the pre-2011 credit cycle.
limitations: Portugal revised its 2021–2025 population series using a new administrative-data methodology, so demographic comparisons must use consistent vintages.
Second-quarter 2026 GDP was revised after the flash estimate; observed quarterly data and annual forecasts are kept separate.
PRR milestone completion and payment requests do not directly measure completed productive capital or long-run productivity effects.
Housing transaction prices and new-contract rents do not by themselves measure affordability.
Renewable electricity shares cannot be extrapolated to total final energy consumption.
The ENTSO-E blackout report describes a multi-factor interconnected-system event and should not be reduced to a single-country or single-technology cause.
The NATO 2% accounting measure does not directly measure operational readiness or domestic defence-industry output.

Revision 1 corrects the Q2 2026 year-on-year GDP figure to the current INE value of 2.5% and adds the required evidence-bearing geographic map in both locales; the broader analytical thesis is unchanged.

selection_rationale: The public corpus contains a focused study of Israel's 1985 stabilization but lacks a reusable country-level dossier linking state formation, constitutional institutions, security mobilisation, high technology, defence industry, fiscal capacity, demographics, energy and water systems, regional normalisation, and the economic mechanisms connecting Israel with the West Bank and Gaza. contrary_evidence: Large foreign-exchange reserves, a resilient financial system, strong high-tech exports and repeated post-shock recoveries argue against a simple thesis of economic fragility.
Rising debt, repeated reserve mobilisation, infrastructure gaps and relocation of some R&D activity abroad argue against treating wartime resilience as costless or indefinitely self-renewing.

Peace treaties and regional normalisation demonstrate substantial interstate integration, while the unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict and continuing regional military confrontation limit any claim that geopolitical risk has structurally disappeared.
A young population can enlarge future labour supply, but uneven employment and skill formation across rapidly growing groups mean demographic growth is not automatically a fiscal dividend.
limitations: Israeli and Palestinian statistical systems use different territorial coverage; population and GDP series must not be combined without explicit scope reconciliation.
Wartime fiscal and defence figures use different accounting perimeters and are frequently revised as operations and reserves change.
Active-conflict casualty, damage and displacement figures can be incomplete or differently defined across Israeli, Palestinian and UN sources.
The ICJ source is an advisory opinion with separate and dissenting opinions; its legal conclusions are attributed precisely and not treated as a negotiated political settlement.
Current macroeconomic forecasts are highly conditional on security assumptions and differ between the IMF and Bank of Israel.
The 27 October 2026 election had not occurred by the evidence cutoff, so no electoral outcome is inferred.

The dossier avoids duplicating the conflict-history report and instead focuses on the internal political economy and reconstruction mechanisms required by current and future research.
contrary_evidence: Ukraine's massive physical damage, demographic displacement and dependence on official finance argue against treating wartime institutional continuity as evidence of normal economic conditions.
Functioning banks, continued exports, domestic defence production, digital administration and progress toward EU accession argue against a state-collapse narrative.

Large reconstruction needs create investment opportunity but do not guarantee growth because security risk, governance, labour supply, insurance and project execution determine whether capital becomes productive capacity.
limitations: Population, labour-force and migration denominators are unusually uncertain under occupation, displacement and wartime administrative conditions.
The 2026 state budget was materially amended during the year; original and amended defence and deficit figures describe different fiscal envelopes.
RDNA5 damage and reconstruction estimates have a 31 December 2025 cutoff and therefore exclude subsequent destruction.
Defence-industry capacity and procurement shares are official operational figures rather than independently audited national accounts.
IMF and NBU forecasts remain highly conditional on security assumptions and external-financing continuity.

A revisão 1 corrige exclusivamente localização editorial e unidades da edição PT-BR após rejeição de QA; as proposições factuais e o conteúdo analítico permanecem materialmente equivalentes à versão inglesa.

selection_rationale: Hong Kong is undergoing a structural transition in which deeper integration with Mainland China's capital markets, technology system and spatial planning is occurring alongside continued operation of a separate currency, open capital account, tax system, customs territory and common-law commercial architecture. Strong 2025-26 capital-market recovery, a new infrastructure-and-technology planning cycle, demographic migration offsets and post-2020 institutional changes interact across economy, politics and society, making the case materially consequential and not reducible to a conventional country profile.
contrary_evidence: Strong IPO fundraising and turnover in 2025-26 contradict a simple claim that post-2020 political and legal changes mechanically caused financial collapse; they do not demonstrate that institutional change has zero economic cost.

Mainland integration expands issuer and investor flows through Stock Connect, Bond Connect and other schemes, while simultaneously increasing concentration in Mainland corporate activity and exposure to Mainland-specific risks.
The HKD peg imports U.S. monetary conditions and constrains domestic rate policy, but it also provides a credible currency anchor that remains central to international financial intermediation.

Residential property has broadly stabilised, while office and retail commercial property continue to face structural vacancy and refinancing pressure; 'the property market' cannot be treated as one cycle.
Population has returned to modest growth because of net inflows, but deaths exceed births and ageing continues to depress labour-force participation.
The Northern Metropolis creates large new technology and industrial capacity on paper, but private firm location, production scale and commercialisation outcomes remain unproven.
limitations: Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China rather than a sovereign state; the ISO code HK is used only for territorial indexing in the research taxonomy.
Official HKSAR and PRC sources establish laws, institutional design and stated policy rationales but are not independent measures of political rights or social effects.
External rights organisations provide documented cases and attributed critical interpretations but do not independently measure the full economic impact of national-security legislation.
Market activity cannot be used as a proxy for institutional legitimacy, and political criticism cannot be used as a proxy for financial decline.
Visa approvals do not equal resident retention or employment, and Northern Metropolis plans do not equal operating industrial capacity.
The IMF's May 2026 growth forecast predates stronger official second-quarter data; the report keeps the forecast and subsequent observations temporally distinct.

selection_rationale: Published canonical research already treats Temasek and Singapore's sovereign-capital architecture as a material transmission mechanism, but the corpus lacks country-level context connecting reserves, CPF, public housing, land, monetary policy, logistics, finance, industrial upgrading, foreign labour, demography and external strategy. This dossier supplies that reusable structural context without duplicating the existing actor studies.
contrary_evidence: Singapore's high gross public-debt ratio is not evidence of conventional fiscal distress because the Government reports a positive net asset position and most borrowing proceeds cannot finance recurrent spending; gross liabilities still require prudent management.
Public housing supports unusually broad owner-occupation, while 99-year lease decay, affordability and CPF withdrawals create genuine intergenerational and retirement trade-offs.
Foreign labour materially expands productive capacity, but it also creates a segmented labour market and additional housing, transport and social-integration pressures.

Singapore's port, financial and legal ecosystems are dense and difficult to reproduce quickly, while neighbouring economies continue improving infrastructure, talent and direct-connectivity alternatives.

Semiconductor investment is structurally important, but Singapore does not control the global leading-edge logic foundry chokepoint and remains heavily dependent on multinational firms and imported technology.

Deep security ties with the United States and deep economic relations with China coexist; the evidence supports issue-specific diversification rather than simple geopolitical equidistance or exclusive alignment.
limitations: The total value of Singapore's national reserves is not publicly disclosed, and GIC does not disclose assets under management; third-party AUM estimates should not be treated as official figures.
Temasek's publicly reported net portfolio value is not equivalent to the stock of national reserves.
EDB fixed-asset-investment commitments are expected projects and should not be treated as already-realised investment.
The 6 GW low-carbon electricity-import target is planned capacity for 2035, not operating supply today.
Population statistics distinguish citizens, permanent residents and non-residents; total population alone obscures labour-market, infrastructure and political implications.

Political and civil-liberties assessments use source classes with different functions: official sources establish laws and institutional design, while external rights organisations provide attributed criticism and case-based evidence.

selection_rationale: Taiwan is undergoing a consequential structural transition in which an AI-driven export boom, further concentration of leading-edge semiconductor production, a sharp reorientation of export demand toward the United States, demographic contraction, energy-security constraints and persistent cross-Strait military pressure are increasingly interacting. contrary_evidence: The U.S. overtook mainland China and Hong Kong combined as Taiwan's largest export destination in 2025, but cross-Strait trade, investment and production networks remain large; the evidence supports rebalancing rather than decoupling.

Competitive elections, alternation in power and constitutional review support institutional resilience, while divided government and budget disputes show that democratic checks can also slow policy execution.
Semiconductor concentration creates strong global incentives to avoid disruption, but there is no empirical basis for treating the so-called silicon shield as an automatic military deterrent.

limitations: The legal and diplomatic status of Taiwan is contested. The research separates effective administration, constitutional claims, diplomatic recognition and institutional participation rather than adopting one actor's sovereignty formulation as fact.

PRC, Taiwan, U.S. and other official security statements are strategic communications as well as policy evidence; intentions are not inferred mechanically from military-activity counts or official rhetoric.
Semiconductor capacity and trade concentration are observable, but their effect on deterrence and crisis decisions is inferential.
Long-run demographic figures are conditional projections based on fertility, mortality and migration assumptions, not deterministic forecasts.
Military readiness, ammunition stocks, classified intelligence and crisis plans cannot be independently measured from public data with the same precision as macroeconomic or trade variables.
Exceptional 2025-2026 GDP and export growth reflects a concentrated AI and semiconductor cycle and should not be extrapolated mechanically as Taiwan's long-run trend growth.
